summary: Regolith is a browser game where students design and run a Moon or Mars outpost for 60 sols, balancing power, radiation shielding, life support, food and mass. Every choice has a cost, and a post-mortem traces failures to the decision that caused them. A rover mission layer logs open, structured data that can train rover navigation and planning AI.
details:
What it is. Regolith is a browser game where students design and run a Moon or Mars outpost for 60 sols. Before launch, players split a fixed mass budget across solar arrays, fission units, batteries, radiation shielding, life-support recycling, greenhouse beds and stored rations. Then they run the outpost, spending 12 crew-hours per sol on greenhouse tending, life-support maintenance, panel cleaning, regolith excavation, a rover EVA, or hibernate mode, while random events strike: solar particle events, recycler faults, dust build-up, and Martian dust storms. Three sites change the constraints: Moon (polar ridge), Moon (equatorial, with a 14-day night) and Mars. If the mission fails, a post-mortem traces the failure back to specific decisions with numbers.

How it works. One deterministic resource model links power, oxygen, water, food, radiation dose, dust and mass, so no choice is free. A rover EVA minigame adds scouting (tagging rocks and craters), terrain driving with slope, tilt and battery drain, and a self-righting decision after a tip-over. Everything runs in a single HTML/JavaScript file with canvas graphics and needs no install.

NASA data and resources. Our life-support model is parameterized with NASA published values: crew oxygen use from NASA’s Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD), baseline drinking water intake and food planning values from NASA Johnson Space Center and NTRS publications, and Mars surface radiation from the Curiosity rover’s Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD) measurements. [Add only the sources you finish verifying; see below.]

Benefits and impact. Students feel why a mission fails or succeeds instead of reading about it. The same simulation produces open, structured data, with every outpost decision, rover drive trace, hazard label and self-righting choice stored as JSONL. This data is intended to train rover navigation, perception and planning AI, and to benchmark resource-allocation agents. It supports high-level policy and perception, not low-level servo control. Our own rover project is the first user of the data.

Creativity. The game is both a learning tool and a data-collection pipeline: each lesson a student learns also becomes labelled human-decision data.

Tools. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, canvas, Google Fonts, GitHub Pages. The code was generated with Claude (Anthropic) AI and edited by our team; the concept and rover integration are ours.

Factors we considered. Scientific accuracy vs playability (simplified physics, real parameters), mobile controls for classrooms, privacy (anonymous data only, no personal information), honest limits of what game data can teach a robot, and a roadmap: real LRO and HiRISE imagery for hazard labelling, cloud collection across schools, and a digital twin of our rover.
dataRefs: NASA NTRS: Life support inputs and outputs per crew member per day (oxygen 0.84 kg)
NASA NTRS: Astronaut mass balance and water values for exploration missions (Ewert and Stromgren, 2019)
NASA Curiosity rover RAD: Mars surface radiation measurements (Hassler et al., Science, 2013)
NASA Curiosity rover RAD results, press release (0.67 mSv/day on the Martian surface)
